newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korean troops suffering in famine -- congressman.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean troops suffering in famine -- congressman.

text.p: A U.S. congressman just back from North Korea said on Tuesday he saw soldiers whose uniforms hung off their bodies, showing that even the communist nation's military is not immune from the "hell of severe famine".
"North Korea is rapidly descending into a hell of severe famine," U.S. Congressman Tony Hall told reporters in Tokyo after returning from a four-day tour of North Korea.

Hall, who toured North Korea from April 4 to 7 on a humanitarian fact-finding mission for the U.S. government, said he was given unprecedented freedom to make "unannounced stops" in areas between Pyongyang and the Yalu River border city of Sinuiju, where he saw soldiers and civilians suffering alike.
"You look at the soldiers and their uniforms don't fit," he told a news conference at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo. "Everyone is systematically starving together."

Hall gave a bleak account of wide areas of northwestern North Korea where gaunt women and children scrounged for "anything that looked edible" in depleted soil in a landscape where every tree had been cut down for firewood.

Many countries have been slow to respond to international appeals for food aid to North Korea, in part out of fears donations would go to the 1.1 million-strong armed forces, which consume about a quarter of the impoverished state's budget and is massed menacingly close to the border with South Korea.
Hall acknowledged the international community's distaste and distrust for North Korea and its closed society and political system, but said "food doesn't have to go to the government".
He cited Pyongyang's assurances that aid and church groups would be able to monitor distribution of food and signs that the government was spreading rations evenly.

"The government is trying to do everything it can to give everybody a little food," Hall said, contrasting North Korea with African states where he said thousands had died from a complete lack of food.
But Hall said conditions were far worse in North Korea now than when he last visited in August.
"What the world has promised and committed to as far as food North Korea is not enough -- it's not even close," said the Ohio Democrat, a hunger specialist.
His delegation included a humanitarian disaster expert from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control.
Relief has begun to trickle into North Korea, whose food shortages are partly the result of two consecutive years of crop-killing floods.
In a new burst of activity, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said last week it would double its latest appeal for food aid for North Korea to 203,000 tons.

On Monday, the giant U.S. grain trader Cargill Inc. announced it had reached agreement with the North Koreans for the supply of an undisclosed amount of U.S. wheat, marking its first commercial sale of American grain to the regime.
The WFP, which has determined North Korea needs 2.3 million tonnes of food this year, in February appealed for $41.6 million to help Pyongyang stave off hunger.
The United States has pledged $10 million and South Korea $6 million in a response to the appeal.
Hall said he planned to press Tokyo to dip into its huge rice reserves to help North Korea.
On Monday, Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said Tokyo would not help its former colony until the communist government answers charges that it abducted a Japanese girl in 1977.
